text:
B: Hello.
A: Hello. Can you hear me all right?
B: Yes. I'm Abena.
A: Alison. Nice to meet you. I'm in Stockton-on-Tees.
B: Crawley. Near Gatwick.
A: Oh, you'll be well placed for holidays, then.
B: You'd think. I've just said this to someone. Ten minutes from the airport and I still only fly at Christmas, when it costs the most.
A: I'm the same with the coast, really. It's not far, and I hardly go.
B: What do you do?
A: I'm retired. I was a medical secretary at a GP practice for twenty-seven years.
B: Oh. Okay. So you were on the other side of the phone from me.
A: Sorry, how do you mean?
B: I'm a pharmacy technician. Half my day is ringing GP surgeries saying, this script is wrong, this dose doesn't make sense, can the doctor look at it. And they put me on hold.
A: Oh dear. I probably did put a few people like you on hold, if I'm honest. But I'd always get the doctor to look at it in the end. It was the ones who shouted that waited longest.
B: That's fair, actually. I'd do the same.
A: We had a pharmacist down the road who'd ring about every little thing, and he was usually right, which was the annoying part.
B: Yes. We're usually right.
A: I'm sure you are.
B: Do you miss it?
A: Erm, I miss the people a bit. Not the phones. I walk along the river most mornings now, and I do the coffee morning at church once a month.
B: Church, okay. Which?
A: Just the parish church. Church of England. It's very quiet. I mostly go for the familiar faces, if that makes sense.
B: It does. Mine's Methodist, Ghanaian congregation. Nothing quiet about it. Two and a half hours on a good day.
A: Goodness. Ours is an hour and people start looking at their watches.
B: An hour? I'd still be finding a parking space. What happens at the coffee morning?
A: Oh, tea, tray bakes. I always do a lemon drizzle. I'm quite proud of it, actually. It goes first.
B: You should be. I don't bake at all. I cook, big pots, jollof, soup, but baking, no. The kids get shop cake.
A: How old are they?
B: Thirteen and nine. The boy lives on his PlayStation.
A: Mine's thirty-one and he's moved back home, so I wouldn't count on that changing.
B: Don't tell me that.
A: Sorry. He's a good lad. He works shifts at a warehouse, so I never know whether I'm doing his tea early or late.
B: At least he works.
A: Yes, there is that. I try not to nag him.
B: That's hard. I'm a nagger. I know I am.
A: Well, someone has to be, with a thirteen-year-old. I'd have taken the PlayStation off my two, if we'd had them then.
